notes.title: Start here: follow one usage event through MeterForge
notes.body:
MeterForge is a C# billing app. This course follows one business fact: "subscription S used quantity Q of meter M at time T". A client reports that fact with an HTTP POST, and because networks fail, the same fact can arrive more than once. The whole course is about keeping "a request" and "a fact" apart.

Suggested reading order (all in `astraupskill/`):

1. `README.md`: the glossary table. Learn the words *entity identity*, *request identity*, *replay*, *winner* and *idempotency conflict* before anything else.
2. `01-CODEBASE-MAP.md`: read the listed files in order and follow the values named `candidate`, then `stored`, then `response`.
3. `02-CONCEPTS.md`: identity, retries, atomic operations, error codes, and how the design maps to SQL. Most quizzes in this pack come from here, so read it slowly and predict each outcome before reading the answer.
4. `03-WORKED-CHANGE.md` and `04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md`: the actual repair and the tests that prove it.
5. `05-PRACTICE.md`, then `06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md` only after you tried.

excerpts.quote: a request and a fact are different things: a network retry can produce a second request for the same fact.
Follow the value called `candidate`, then `stored`, then `response`.

readMore.why: The glossary that names each idea and points to where it lives in the code.
The file-by-file request path with one question to answer per file.

notes.title: Core idea: the stored id and the caller's key are different things
notes.body:
Every stored usage event has two kinds of identity, and mixing them up causes most retry bugs.

- **Entity identity** is the id the server assigns to the event when it builds it. The client never chooses it.
- **Request identity** is the external event ID the *client* sends. Together with the tenant, it forms the storage key `(TenantId, ExternalEventId)`. It exists so a client can send the same fact again when it does not know whether the first attempt arrived.

Look at the small table in the concepts chapter and predict each row before reading its right-hand side. Notice that the tenant is part of the key, so two tenants can use the same external ID without touching each other.

The second idea in the chapter is that *validation* (is this input allowed?), *normalization* (what is the canonical form, such as trimmed text and UTC time?) and *equality* (is this the same business fact?) are three separate decisions. Keep them apart in your head when you read the `UsageEvent` constructor.

excerpts.quote: The storage key is the pair `(TenantId, ExternalEventId)`.

```text tenant-a + evt-1 + quantity 10 -> created E1 tenant-a + evt-1 + quantity 10 -> replay E1 tenant-a + evt-1 + quantity 11 -> conflict; E1 remains 10 tenant-b + evt-1 + quantity 10 -> created E2 tenant-a + evt-2 + quantity 10 -> created E3 ```
Validation asks whether the input is allowed: nonempty IDs, nonblank fields and a positive quantity.

readMore.why: The constructor where validation and normalization happen.

notes.title: Core idea: one store operation chooses the winner
notes.body:
When two requests with the same key arrive at the same moment, only one event may end up stored. The course calls it the *winner*. The repaired code picks the winner in a single store call, `GetOrAddAsync`, which in memory is `ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd`: "store this if the key is free, otherwise give me what is already there".

Then the service compares the stored event with the candidate it just built. If the business data differs, it throws the `usage.idempotency_conflict` error. If the stored id is not the candidate's id, someone else got there first, so this call is a replay.

Read the old sequence in section 3 of the concepts chapter (find, then add) and its timeline table. Ask: each step is thread-safe, so why is the *sequence* not? That question, and what changes when the same idea moves to a Postgres table (section 7), carries most of this pack.

excerpts.quote: var stored = _events.GetOrAdd((candidate.TenantId, candidate.ExternalEventId), candidate);
return new UsageIngestionResult(stored, stored.Id != candidate.Id);
## 3. A thread-safe collection does not make a sequence atomic

readMore.why: The whole ingestion service: build the candidate, get-or-add, compare, report replay.
Why the concurrency test is built the way it is, and how to break the change on purpose.

notes.title: Why a retry with a fresh external ID creates a second event
notes.body:
The server can only recognise a retry by its key. The key is the tenant plus the external event ID. If the client loses the response and then sends the same quantity with a *newly generated* ID, it is telling the server "this is another fact". So the server creates a second event, and the guide says that is correct under the contract. The fix belongs on the client: keep the same key until that logical action is resolved. Idempotency is a contract between client and server, not magic that makes any duplicate request safe.

- **Server-side idempotency bug:** the server did what the key told it; the client broke its half of the contract.
- **Detects the duplicate by payload:** the server looks up by key only. It never searches for matching payloads under other keys.
- **409:** a 409 needs the *same* key with different data. Here the key is new.

excerpts.quote: Generating a new external ID on the retry tells the server this is another fact, so two creations would be correct under the contract.
Idempotency is a client-and-server contract, not a header that makes arbitrary duplicate requests safe.

notes.title: What the DO UPDATE SET id = id trick costs
notes.body:
`ON CONFLICT ... DO NOTHING RETURNING *` returns no row when the key is taken, so some teams use a fake update instead: `DO UPDATE SET id = usage_events.id`. It changes nothing, but because it counts as an update, `RETURNING` fires and you get the row back. The guide's warning: this is a real write, so every replay takes a row lock. On a hot idempotency key, where retries pile up, that forces exactly those replays to wait on each other. The guide says it serialises the traffic "you least want to serialize".

- **A second round trip:** both forms are a single statement; the extra cost is a write and lock, not a network trip.
- **Losing stored values:** `SET id = usage_events.id` writes back the same id, so the stored data is unchanged.
- **A full table scan:** the conflict is found through the unique constraint, and the guide says nothing about scans.

excerpts.quote: An alternative some teams prefer is `ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, external_event_id) DO UPDATE SET id = usage_events.id RETURNING *` — a deliberate no-op update purely to make `RETURNING` fire. It is shorter, and it costs you a write and a row lock on every replay, which on a hot idempotency key is exactly the traffic you least want to serialize. Know both; choose on purpose.

readMore.why: The DO NOTHING plus UNION ALL form the guide prefers, and why.

notes.title: Why a unique-violation catch must name the constraint
notes.body:
With a plain `INSERT`, a duplicate key makes Postgres raise a unique-violation error (`SqlState == "23505"`). If you treat that error as "this was a replay", you must make sure it came from the idempotency key, `usage_events_idempotency`. Otherwise a *different* unique index (added later for some other rule) would also raise 23505, and your code would wrongly report a real failure as a harmless replay. The guide also says to prefer `ON CONFLICT`, which never raises at all.

- **The table name:** many constraints can live on one table, so the table name does not tell you which rule was broken.
- **Any 23505:** that is the exact mistake the guide warns about.
- **The full DbUpdateException message:** message text is not the stable signal; the guide names the constraint name as the thing to match.

excerpts.quote: If you use plain `INSERT` plus a catch, you must match on the **constraint name**, not on "any unique violation" — a second unique index would otherwise be reported as an idempotent replay.
CONSTRAINT usage_events_idempotency UNIQUE (tenant_id, external_event_id)

notes.title: Which status an identical replay gets, and why
notes.body:
The course gives each outcome its own status code so a client can react differently. An identical replay, same tenant, same key and same business data, gets **200**: "this already succeeded, here is the original event". That is different from **201**, which means a new event was created just now. A retry can therefore return 200 after the first attempt returned 201 without breaking idempotency: the same stored event comes back both times.

- **409:** reserved for a reused key carrying *different* business data.
- **202:** not part of this contract at all; nothing is accepted for later processing.
- **201:** only for the call that actually created the event.

For the full list the guide also gives 422 (domain validation failure) and 404 (unknown event in a tenant-scoped lookup).

excerpts.quote: This change uses 201 for a new event, 200 for an identical replay, 409 for a reused key with changed business data, 422 for domain validation failures, and 404 for an unknown tenant-scoped event lookup.

readMore.why: Where the endpoint turns the replay flag into a status code.

notes.title: Why the outbox row can't just follow GetOrAdd
notes.body:
A replay must be silent: same response, no new event, and no new audit or outbox row. If the adapter always inserted an outbox row after calling `GetOrAdd`, every replay would add one, and a retried request could emit a duplicate billing event. So the adapter has to know whether *this* call created the event. The `WITH inserted AS (...)` SQL form gives that for free: the `inserted` part is empty on a replay. The guide adds that all side effects belong in one transaction with the insert.

- **Outbox before the event:** the guide puts them in the same transaction; it never requires outbox-first.
- **A different database:** the guide says the opposite, one transaction for the insert and its side effects.
- **GetOrAdd keeps a lock:** nothing in the guide says it holds a lock afterwards; the problem is knowing created versus replayed.

excerpts.quote: All of it in **one** transaction with the insert, and none of it repeated on a replay.
So the adapter cannot simply "insert the outbox row after calling `GetOrAdd`" — it has to know whether the insert actually created anything.

notes.title: What ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING * gives on a taken key
notes.body:
When the key already exists, `DO NOTHING` does nothing, and `RETURNING *` only returns rows that were actually inserted. So it returns **zero rows**. It does not hand back the existing row. The guide calls this the most common surprise. That is why the statement has a second branch: `UNION ALL` a `SELECT` of the existing row, guarded by `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM inserted)`. Both branches run in one statement, so there is no gap between "did it exist?" and "then insert".

- **A 23505 error:** `ON CONFLICT` handles the conflict in SQL, so it does not raise.
- **The existing row, like GetOrAdd:** that is the surprise the guide warns about; the extra branch is needed to get it.
- **The new row, overwriting:** `DO NOTHING` never writes over the stored row.

excerpts.quote: ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT usage_events_idempotency DO NOTHING RETURNING * ) SELECT * FROM inserted UNION ALL
`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING *` returns **zero rows** when the key was already taken — it does not return the existing row

notes.title: What a single GetOrAdd call does and does not guarantee
notes.body:
`GetOrAdd` is the one place where a key becomes tied to an event: it either stores the candidate or returns the event already stored, as one indivisible act. Every caller then reasons about that same stored winner. The guide is careful about the limit: this is atomicity *for this one process*. The dictionary lives in memory inside one running API instance.

- **Exactly-once billing downstream:** the guide says it is "not a distributed exactly-once guarantee", and side effects like outbox rows are a separate problem.
- **Exactly-once across every replica:** a second API instance has its own dictionary; the guide says the in-memory version "cannot coordinate two API instances at all".
- **Survives restarts:** memory is lost on restart; the guide lists "Restart forgets every key" as the reason to move to a database.

excerpts.quote: This is the atomicity guarantee for this one process; it is not a distributed exactly-once guarantee.
var stored = _events.GetOrAdd((candidate.TenantId, candidate.ExternalEventId), candidate);
The in-memory version cannot deduplicate a retry that arrives after the process has lost its state, and cannot coordinate two API instances at all

notes.title: Why counting stored rows could not reveal the old race
notes.body:
In the old find-then-add flow, two requests both read "missing". Request A inserts E1. Request B's insert of E2 loses because the key now exists, but the old adapter ignored `TryAdd`'s result, so B still returned "created E2". Storage holds one row, which looks perfect if you only count rows. The bug is in what the *callers* were told: B handed out an identity that was never stored. So tests must also check the returned identities and the created/replay flags.

- **A cached count:** nothing in the guide involves caching the count.
- **Both events dropped:** step 3 of the table shows E1 was inserted, so the count is one, not zero.
- **Both events stored:** step 4 shows E2's insert lost; only one row was stored.

excerpts.quote: | 3 | Inserts E1 | | | 4 | | Insert E2 loses because key exists | | 5 | Returns created E1 | Returns created E2 even though E2 was never stored |

The old adapter ignored `TryAdd`'s result, so the caller could receive an identity that was not actually in storage. Counting stored rows alone would miss this bug. You must also check the identities and creation/replay flags returned to callers.

readMore.why: How the concurrency test checks identities and flags, not just counts.

notes.title: Why evt-1 with a new quantity is a 409
notes.body:
The second request has the same tenant and the same external key as E1, but different business data (quantity 11 instead of 10). The server finds E1 under that key and compares subscription, meter, quantity and time. They differ, so the service throws `usage.idempotency_conflict`, which becomes a 409. E1 is not touched and still says 10. The guide's table shows this row: "conflict; E1 remains 10".

- **A new event E2:** a new event needs a new key (or another tenant); this key is taken.
- **Replay with quantity updated to 11:** stored events are never changed by a replay; `UsageEvent` is immutable.
- **Replay ignoring the quantity:** a replay must be the *same* fact; quietly ignoring a changed quantity would hide a real disagreement.

excerpts.quote: tenant-a + evt-1 + quantity 10 -> created E1 tenant-a + evt-1 + quantity 10 -> replay E1 tenant-a + evt-1 + quantity 11 -> conflict; E1 remains 10
stored.Quantity != candidate.Quantity

notes.title: Why the internal GUID is left out of the replay comparison
notes.body:
Every time the service handles a request it builds a fresh candidate with `Guid.NewGuid()`. So the candidate's GUID never matches the stored one, even for a perfect retry. Comparing GUIDs would turn every replay into a conflict. That is why the comparison covers only subscription, meter, quantity and occurrence time. The service actually uses the GUID the other way round: `stored.Id != candidate.Id` is how it knows this call was a replay.

- **Subscription id:** compared; a different subscription under the same key is a conflict even if the quantity matches.
- **Meter name:** compared (`stored.Meter != candidate.Meter`).
- **Occurrence time:** compared, after normalizing to UTC, so equal instants written with different offsets still match.

excerpts.quote: Internal GUID is intentionally excluded because each proposed insertion starts with a new GUID.
var candidate = new UsageEvent(Guid.NewGuid(), tenantId, subscriptionId, meter, quantity, occurredAt, externalEventId);
if (stored.SubscriptionId != candidate.SubscriptionId || stored.Meter != candidate.Meter || stored.Quantity != candidate.Quantity || stored.OccurredAt != candidate.OccurredAt)

notes.title: What a client should do with a 409
notes.body:
A 409 here means "this key already names a *different* fact". Sending the same conflicting payload again cannot fix that: the stored event will not change, so every retry will get the same 409. The guide says the client should keep the user's draft and show a useful action, so a person can decide what to do. Retrying with the same ID is right only for an *uncertain network outcome*, such as a lost response, which is the case idempotency exists for.

- **Retry with backoff until it answers 200:** it never will; the conflict is permanent for that key.
- **New ID and resend immediately:** that tells the server it is a new fact, and could create a second event the user did not mean to create.
- **Treat 409 like 200:** the stored event is a different fact, so pretending it succeeded hides the disagreement.

excerpts.quote: Do not retry every non-200 response automatically. Repeating the same conflicting payload will not repair an idempotency conflict. A client should preserve its draft and show a useful action.

readMore.why: Exercise 3 asks you to build exactly this conflict-aware client.

notes.title: Why the tenant in the route is not authorization
notes.body:
The tenant id in the URL tells the server *which namespace* to look in. It does not tell the server *who is asking*. Authorization needs an authenticated principal (a logged-in identity) plus a check that this principal may access that tenant. MeterForge's events are scoped by tenant, but nothing proves the caller belongs to it. The guide asks you to keep these two concepts separate in every CRUD app.

- **A hard-to-guess tenant value:** a secret-looking name is still not a proof of identity; anyone who learns it can use it.
- **The 404 makes it equivalent:** a 404 for unknown events only hides *other* tenants' ids from this tenant's lookups; it does not stop someone from using a tenant they do not belong to.
- **The URL tenant proves membership:** the caller can type any tenant into a URL.

excerpts.quote: the route identifies the namespace, but no authenticated principal proves access to it.
| tenant scope | the tenant id in the route and in every key; scoping is not authorization | the `tenantId` route parameter in `src/MeterForge.Api/Usage/UsageEndpoints.cs` |

notes.title: Why the tenant string is not lowercased or trimmed
notes.body:
The guide treats the tenant as an *opaque* identity: the system does not interpret it, it just compares it exactly. Normalizing every string "to be safe" is dangerous, because two identifiers that differ only in case can be two different resources, and lowercasing would merge them into one. The rule is to decide each normalization at the right contract boundary and test it. For external event IDs and meters the contract chose trimming; for tenants it did not.

- **Tenants are GUIDs:** the tenant is a string (`tenant-a`, `tenant-b` in the examples), not a GUID; only the stored event's internal id is a GUID.
- **Breaks the dictionary's hash:** a `ConcurrentDictionary` works with any string key, lowercased or not.
- **A regex rejects whitespace:** the guide mentions no such tenant regex.

excerpts.quote: The tenant string is treated as an opaque identity and is not automatically lowercased or trimmed here.
Do not normalize every string indiscriminately: two case-sensitive external identifiers can be different resources.

notes.title: Why looking up " evt-1 " but storing "evt-1" was a bug
notes.body:
An idempotency check only works if the key you *look up* is the same key you *store*. The old flow looked up the raw string with spaces, `" evt-1 "`, which never matched anything, and then the constructor trimmed it and stored `"evt-1"`. One operation used two different keys, so a retry with stray spaces could look like a brand-new creation. The fix is ordering: the service now builds the candidate event first (the constructor validates and normalizes) and only then uses its key for `GetOrAddAsync`.

- **Case-insensitive lookup:** the problem was whitespace, and the guide never describes a case-insensitive lookup.
- **Trimming is forbidden:** the opposite; the constructor deliberately trims external event IDs.
- **Whitespace makes the dictionary throw:** a string with spaces is a valid key; it just is a *different* key.

excerpts.quote: The service constructs the candidate event before selecting its key.

// Validate and normalize before choosing the idempotency key. var candidate = new UsageEvent(Guid.NewGuid(), tenantId, subscriptionId, meter, quantity, occurredAt, externalEventId); var stored = await store.GetOrAddAsync(candidate, cancellationToken).ConfigureAwait(false);

readMore.why: Step 2 of the worked change: normalize before choosing the key.
